comments.why: Explains electrons as waves of an underlying field.
comments.text: All of this makes more sense when understood in terms of Field theory: David Tong: Quantum Fields [VIDEO] "All the electrons that are in your body are not fundamental. All the electrons that exist in your body are waves of the same underlying field." The next question is, if there are no individual things, what does math count? [LINK]

comments.author: Agamus
comments.why: Tong lecture arguing there are no particles, only waves.
comments.text: Agreed - mathematics is predicated on the idea that there are individual things, but as we are learning, through things like quantum field theory, there are no individual things, hence, no individuated 'things' to count. As such, mathematics is not the 'language of nature'. Check out David Tang's lecture on QFT: "there are no particles, only waves" [VIDEO] Mathematics still works (at our scale); the consequence is precision. Individuation of anything is a construct - including subjects and objects: [LINK]

I believe this guy even talks about it a bit in this video made by the Royal Institution (which I really enjoy watching), discussing the possibility of different fundamental building blocks of nature. comments.author: Agamus
comments.story: Ten years after the Higgs, physicists face the nightmare of finding nothing else
comments.why: Quantum field theory suggests there are no individual things.
comments.text: I think this is correct. My sense is that the assumption of _individuation_ is at the core of logic, which then infects all rational thinking. (We add the predicates to "things", and then forget that we added them!) If there are no individual things, as quantum field theory seems to suggest, what are numbers counting? [VIDEO] [LINK]

comments.author: ianai
comments.story: Any single galaxy reveals the composition of an entire universe
comments.why: Tong clip hinting at holographic relationships in the universe.
comments.text: The cosmological background radiation, which is an image of the universe shortly after the big bang and before inflation, looks similar to the current layout of matter across the universe. This would seem consistent with a universe being able to be extrapolated from a region of it if there's some underlying holographic relationships. Based on this clip from David Tong. Starts here and goes on a few minutes: [VIDEO]
